title: Post-quantum timed release with a sequentiality theorem

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a verifiable delay function whose required sequential work remains resistant to quantum shortcuts, supported by a substantive security theorem. A verifiable delay function takes an input and a chosen work parameter, produces an output after a prescribed sequence of computation, and lets others check that output substantially faster than recomputing it. The goal is to make the delay defensible against a precisely specified quantum adversary, while retaining inexpensive verification.

Lattice-based timed cryptography supplies a concrete research direction: Lai and Malavolta propose that repeatedly applying a standard lattice-based hash function cannot be substantially parallelized. Papercraft subsequently reports an implementation of a lattice-based verifiable delay function with plausible post-quantum security. The envisioned advance would strengthen this direction with a quantum sequentiality reduction under a named, publicly scrutinized assumption. The supplied evidence establishes the research program and reported implementation, but does not establish that this stronger target has been achieved.

significance.text: A convincing construction would provide a verifiable computational timing primitive that remains useful in the presence of the quantum adversaries covered by its theorem. The supplied abstracts identify applications including auctions, lotteries and public randomness. Such systems could use delayed computation to control when an output becomes available, while allowing participants to validate the eventual result cheaply. The significance comes from combining sequential evaluation, quantum resistance and fast verification in one practical construction.

The motivation includes a vulnerability in existing approaches. Lai and Malavolta describe the repeated-squaring sequentiality assumption as failing against quantum adversaries, and the retained Papercraft abstract describes known practical VDF constructions as vulnerable to quantum algorithms. A construction with stronger quantum sequentiality guarantees would address that documented weakness. These abstracts do not establish the specific period-finding attack mechanism asserted in the earlier research text, so that mechanism is not needed to support the impact assessment.

Conditional impact assessment: the cryptographic-clock analogy has limits. Sequential work measures computation, and its duration depends on hardware speed and adversarial resources. Releasing information at a calendar date would therefore require explicit calibration and resource assumptions. Timed encryption would also require an appropriate encryption construction and security argument; a VDF by itself does not encrypt or conceal a message. These additional steps could enable useful timed-release systems, but they are separate obligations from demonstrating a checkable computational delay.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is a quantum sequentiality theorem with meaningful resource bounds at useful delays. Lai and Malavolta introduce a new sequentiality assumption and report concrete evidence and initial cryptanalysis. That supports investigating their construction, but proposing an assumption does not establish its truth. Likewise, an implementation can demonstrate feasible evaluation and verification without establishing resistance to every allowed quantum shortcut. The retained abstracts do not expose enough theorem detail to determine exactly how far the existing results go toward the proposed target.

Proposed scientific requirement: the theorem must connect a successful shortcut to breaking a named assumption, while defining the shortcut precisely. It must specify the task, the meaning of the sequential-work parameter T, quantum gate model, permitted circuit size or width, success probability, preprocessing, memory and other adversarial resources. A depth restriction alone can conceal enormous parallel resources or precomputation. The assumption and reduction must also receive documented public cryptanalysis; merely restating the desired delay as a new sequentiality conjecture would leave the central uncertainty unresolved.

Proposed engineering requirement: a secure parameter regime must deliver substantial evaluation work with much cheaper verification, and the benchmark must make clear what computation and proof costs are included. Hardware differences and implementation improvements must be accounted for when translating work into elapsed time. The earlier blanket claim that lattice problems used for encryption are highly parallel is not established by the supplied abstracts. The narrower issue is whether the particular iterated construction resists the allowed quantum parallel computation.

current_state.text: Lai and Malavolta's Lattice-Based Timed Cryptography is identified in the supplied research as a CRYPTO 2023 publication and is indexed at IACR ePrint 2024/540. Its retained abstract proposes a lattice sequentiality assumption based on repeated application of a standard lattice-based hash function, reports concrete evidence and initial cryptanalysis, and describes a construction template for timed cryptography. This establishes a specific approach and an initial security investigation; the supplied material does not expose the full security model or theorem statements.

Papercraft: Lattice-based Verifiable Delay Function Implemented is identified in the supplied research as an IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2025 publication, with an ePrint record at 2025/879. The retained abstract reports a working lattice-based VDF that verifies almost six minutes of computation in seven seconds, and qualifies its post-quantum security as plausible. Seven seconds relative to almost six minutes is approximately 2% of evaluation time, slightly above 2% if evaluation is below 360 seconds. This is substantially faster than recomputation, but does not meet the candidate's proposed 1% verification threshold. The retained material does not supply the hardware, parameters or complete accounting behind that example.

The Papercraft landing page records a June 2026 revision. Consequently, the retained abstract's wording and timing example cannot automatically be attributed unchanged to the original 2025 publication. Publication identification and the later ePrint revision are distinct pieces of the chronology; the supplied review does not establish which technical details changed between versions.

The supplied review examined two retained landing pages containing abstracts, not the full papers. The source index reports no extraction issues or truncation for those pages, but complete extraction of a landing page does not provide full-paper access. The abstracts do not establish the proposed quantum sequentiality theorem; they also do not justify the categorical claim that neither full paper contains a relevant theorem. The supplied freshness search record is empty, so whether the target remains unmet as of November 1, 2026 is unresolved. These access and freshness limitations do not negate the reported implementation.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance demonstration: evaluate a construction for at least 2^32 sequential steps and verify its output in at most 1% of evaluation time under a specified benchmark. These are candidate-selected targets, not established standards. The demonstration should define a step, connect the step count to measured runtime, disclose hardware and security parameters, and state whether setup, preprocessing, proof generation and data transfer are included. A large step count alone does not establish a useful wall-clock delay.
completion_criteria.label: Evaluate ≥2^32 sequential steps with verification taking ≤1% evaluation time

completion_criteria.text: Proposed theorem requirement: for a precisely defined task requiring T sequential evaluation steps, prove that quantum circuits of depth below T/100 that solve it with a specified success probability would break a named assumption. Define circuit size, gate model, preprocessing, memory, input distribution and adversarial resources so that the reduction has an assessable meaning. The assumption should have documented public review and cryptanalysis. A new conjecture that directly assumes the desired sequentiality would constitute a candidate foundation, rather than completion under this proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Sub-T/100-depth quantum solvers provably break a named, publicly reviewed assumption

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: publish the implementation, benchmark procedure, parameter choices and proof details so independent groups can reproduce the timing and audit the security argument. Demonstrate correctness and verifier behavior across the claimed parameter range, and distinguish measured performance from extrapolation. Finite experiments establish demonstrated breadth; they cannot prove the absence of all quantum shortcuts. Any timed-encryption application should additionally demonstrate its encryption security, while calendar-release claims should specify hardware calibration, resource assumptions and timing uncertainty.
completion_criteria.label: Published artifacts enable independent timing reproduction and security argument audits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CRY-01, A proof that an explicit one-way function exists, and CRY-02, Public-key encryption from one-way functions, concern foundational hardness and encryption. Sequentiality imposes a different demand: a task must resist substantial compression of its computational depth, not merely be hard to invert. An encryption foundation would not by itself establish a delay guarantee, and a VDF would not by itself provide timed encryption.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-03, Practically efficient post-quantum indistinguishability obfuscation, shares the goal of strong cryptographic functionality that survives quantum attack. The supplied abstracts do not establish general obfuscation as an alternative route to this timed-release capability. It remains a possible connection requiring separate evidence, while the proposed direct VDF construction can be assessed without making general obfuscation a prerequisite. CRY-04, General-purpose private computation at near-plaintext cost, and CRY-08, Metadata-private messaging at ordinary cost, concern privacy and efficiency; delayed availability alone supplies neither general computation privacy nor messaging-metadata protection.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-05, Publicly verifiable unclonable money and copy-protected programs, and CRY-06, Practical classical verification of quantum computation, overlap with CRY-09 in their attention to verification and adversaries with quantum capabilities. Their verification targets differ. Checking a delayed output does not establish unclonability or copy protection, and a post-quantum VDF need not involve an honest quantum computation whose execution a classical verifier must certify.

Roster-based synthesis: CRY-07, Position verification that works in physical spacetime, also depends on carefully modeled timing and adversarial resources. Computational sequentiality does not by itself establish physical location or provide a hardware-independent clock. CRY-10, A conclusive quantum classification of deployed lattice encryption, shares questions about lattice assumptions and quantum algorithms. Its encryption-security classification would not automatically settle the sequential depth of an iterated lattice hash. These entries retain distinct objectives and completion requirements.

brief.title: Checkable delays that resist quantum shortcuts
possible: Participants in an auction or lottery could check that a result required a long sequence of computation, even against quantum computers covered by the security proof. Checking the result would take much less work than producing it.
why: Auctions, lotteries and systems that generate public random results could use this delay to control when an output becomes available. Participants could then validate the result cheaply.
Existing practical approaches are vulnerable to quantum algorithms. A construction with a strong security proof would give these systems a firmer basis for trusting their computational delays.

sources.who: Russell W. F. Lai and Giulio Malavolta
sources.showed: They proposed a mathematical assumption that repeatedly applying a particular function cannot be sped up by splitting the work across processors. They presented supporting evidence and an initial search for attacks.
sources.quote: We provide concrete evidence of the validity of this assumption and perform some initial cryptanalysis.
sources.cited_for: A concrete mathematical route to computation that resists parallel shortcuts.
sources.not_established: Supporting a new assumption does not prove that it withstands the quantum shortcuts covered by the proposed breakthrough.

sources.showed: They built Papercraft, a working verifiable delay function: a computation whose result is cheap to check. It uses lattice techniques, mathematical tools with plausible resistance to quantum attacks.
sources.quote: We propose Papercraft, a working implementation of a VDF based entirely on lattice techniques and thus plausibly post-quantum secure.
sources.cited_for: A working implementation with checking substantially faster than computation.
sources.not_established: Plausible quantum resistance and a working implementation do not establish the required proof against quantum shortcuts.

shown: Lai and Malavolta proposed the mathematical foundation and investigated initial attacks. Osadnik and collaborators built Papercraft, demonstrating checking at roughly 2% of computation time. Its resistance to quantum attacks remains described as plausible.
missing: The target requires a proof connecting a successful quantum shortcut to breaking a named mathematical assumption.
That proof must bound parallel computing resources, memory and work done in advance, alongside the shortcut's chance of success.
A practical construction must jointly meet the proposed performance targets and security requirements, with independently reproducible results.

milestones.label: Substantial sequential work with checking below the target cost
milestones.explanation: A benchmark would have to reach the proposed sequential step count while checking takes at most 1% of computation time, with hardware and costs stated. This would demonstrate substantial work with cheap checking.

milestones.label: Quantum shortcuts provably break a publicly scrutinized assumption
milestones.explanation: A proof would have to connect quantum solutions using less than one hundredth of the required sequential depth to breaking a named, publicly scrutinized assumption. Explicit resource limits would make the guarantee meaningful.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce timings and audit the security argument
milestones.explanation: Published code, parameters, benchmarks and proofs would have to support independent timing reproduction and security audits. Correctness checks and explicit limits on encryption and calendar timing would establish practical boundaries.

uncertain: How well does the proposed mathematical assumption withstand public attempts to break it?
What benchmark definitions and quantum resource limits would make the proposed thresholds convincing?
How reliably can computational work translate into elapsed time across different hardware and adversarial resources?

page.title: Post-quantum verifiable delay functions
page.definition: A verifiable delay function maps each input to one correct output that anyone can check much faster than recomputing it. A post-quantum implementation has a theorem, under a named hardness assumption, bounding the chance that a parallel quantum computation learns the output early, even without producing a proof. The bound accounts for work done on the public parameters before the input is known.

goal.need: Ethereum uses shared randomness to choose who may propose a block. The last contributor can bias the draw by withholding its contribution. In one model, a participant with 10% of the stake can thereby propose 10.19% of rounds. If contributions close before anyone can predict the draw, validators cannot choose between outcomes to favor themselves. This requires a source of randomness and a delay that holds even for a quantum computer. The usual delay based on repeated squaring loses that guarantee against quantum order-finding.

completion.title: An implemented VDF has a peer-reviewed quantum sequentiality reduction and fast public verification.
completion.criterion: An implemented VDF has correctness, quantum soundness and quantum sequentiality theorems. After poly(λ,T) quantum preprocessing of the public parameters, a polynomial-size quantum circuit given a fresh random input computes its correct output at depth below an explicit σ(T)<T only with probability negligible in λ. A peer-reviewed reduction to a named quantum hardness assumption quantifies the depth loss and specifies T, σ, gate set, width, memory and preprocessing. Public verification takes poly(λ,log T) time and is measurably faster than evaluation at the same parameters.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; no outside body was found to have published this combined implementation-and-quantum-sequentiality test.
completion.basis: The standard sequentiality game tests the output alone after preprocessing. RootPack specifies quantum soundness for a delay proof. ZKBdf includes proof generation in its sequentiality test. The revised Lai–Malavolta paper leaves quantum security of its proof of sequential work open, and Papercraft reports fast verification with plausible post-quantum security. These results establish different parts of the Atlas test.

milestones.title: A length-N hash sequence resists N−1 rounds of quantum queries to an ideal hash function.
milestones.criterion: Let H map bit strings to λ-bit strings uniformly at random and let δ≥1. A quantum algorithm makes at most q oracle queries in total over N−1 parallel rounds. Its probability of returning (x₀,y₀), …, (xₙ₋₁,yₙ₋₁) and xₙ, with n=N, every |xᵢ|≤δλ and, for each 0≤i<N, yᵢ=H(xᵢ) occurring as a substring of xᵢ₊₁, is at most (64q³δλ+2N)/2^λ.
milestones.set_by: Blocki, Lee and Zhou, ITC 2021, Theorem 3; a peer-reviewed lower bound in the parallel quantum random oracle model.
milestones.threshold_quote: any quantum attacker running in sequential time T-1 will fail to produce an ℋ-sequence except with negligible probability

milestones.title: A VDF implementation verifies its output faster than recomputing it.
milestones.criterion: For the same input and parameter setting, measure the time to compute the output and the time for a public verifier to check it using the proof. Verification must take less time than computing the output. Account for proof generation separately.
milestones.set_by: VDF research community, fast public verification requirement stated by Boneh, Bünz and Fisch in Section 1 of A Survey of Two Verifiable Delay Functions.
milestones.threshold_quote: However once computed, the output can be quickly verified by anyone.

milestones.title: A VDF's evaluation proof has at least 80 bits of soundness in the quantum random oracle model.
milestones.criterion: A candidate's proof of correct evaluation meets the RootPack requirement of at least 80 bits of provable soundness in the quantum random oracle model, which permits hash queries in superposition. This requirement concerns acceptance of incorrect outputs. Completion additionally requires a quantum sequentiality reduction excluding fast computation of correct outputs.
milestones.set_by: RootPack developers at the Ethereum Foundation, Supranational and Johns Hopkins University, Not So Slowth, Section 2.3, requirement 2; published for Ethereum 2.0.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least 80 bits of provable soundness in a quantum random oracle model

milestones.title: A VDF preserves its classical online delay after polynomial-time quantum preprocessing.
milestones.criterion: In the quantum-annoyance game, the adversary first spends poly(T,λ) quantum time on the public parameters. After receiving a uniformly sampled challenge, its classical online algorithm has parallel time less than T. The probability that it returns the correct function output must be negligible in λ.
milestones.set_by: De Feo, Masson, Petit and Sanso, ASIACRYPT 2019, Definition 2, sequentiality and quantum annoyance.
milestones.threshold_quote:
if A0 is allowed a quantum computation in poly(T, λ), we say that
 the VDFs are quantum annoying.
